overview.title: Stacking the samples, building targets, plotting the data
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.subsection: 3.3.2 An end-to-end example: A linear classifier in pure TensorFlow
overview.main_topic: Turning two NumPy point clouds into a single training set (inputs + binary targets) and visualizing it before any model is built.
overview.central_idea: The two classes generated on p.93 are stacked into one `(2000, 2)` float32 input array, a matching `(2000, 1)` array of 0/1 targets is built in the same order, and a scatter plot (figure 3.1) confirms that the two classes form two separate, roughly linearly separable blobs.
overview.importance: Every supervised learning job starts with exactly this step: aligning inputs and labels row by row, with the right shapes and dtypes. The shapes chosen here, `(2000, 2)` and `(2000, 1)`, dictate the shapes of the model variables `W` (2, 1) and `b` (1,) that are created on the next page, and the plot gives a visual sanity check that a linear model should be able to solve the problem.
learning_objectives: Explain what `np.vstack` does and why the result of stacking two `(1000, 2)` arrays is `(2000, 2)`.
Explain why the inputs are cast to `float32` and the targets created with `dtype="float32"`.
Build a label array whose row order matches the input array, and state the shape convention `(num_samples, 1)` used for the targets.
Read listing 3.16: use NumPy slicing to pull out the x and y coordinates and color points by their class with `plt.scatter`.
Interpret figure 3.1 and argue why the two classes look separable by a straight line.

summary:
This page finishes preparing the data for the pure-TensorFlow linear classifier started in section 3.3.2 (p.93).

- **Inputs (listing 3.14).** Listing 3.13 on p.93 produced two NumPy arrays, `negative_samples` and `positive_samples`, each of shape `(1000, 2)`: 1,000 points in the 2D plane per class. `np.vstack` concatenates them along the first axis (rows) to give one array `inputs` of shape `(2000, 2)`. The first 1,000 rows are class 0, the last 1,000 rows are class 1. The result is cast with `.astype(np.float32)` because NumPy's random generators produce `float64`, while TensorFlow variables and operations in this example work in `float32`.
- **Targets (listing 3.15).** The labels are another `vstack`: 1,000 rows of zeros (`np.zeros((num_samples_per_class, 1))`) on top of 1,000 rows of ones, both `float32`, giving `targets` with shape `(2000, 1)`. Because both arrays were stacked in the same order (negatives first), `targets[i, 0]` is 0 exactly when `inputs[i]` belongs to class 0, and 1 otherwise. The trailing axis of size 1 means each target is a length-1 vector, which matches the `(2000, 1)` output that the model `matmul(inputs, W) + b` will produce (p.95).
- **Plot (listing 3.16, figure 3.1).** With Matplotlib (preinstalled in Colab), `plt.scatter(inputs[:, 0], inputs[:, 1], c=targets[:, 0])` draws every point at its (x, y) coordinates and colors it by its label. Figure 3.1 shows two elongated, tilted clouds: one (dark purple) centered near (0, 3) and one (yellow) centered near (3, 0). The clouds touch slightly in the middle but are mostly separated by a diagonal line, which is what makes this a good toy problem for a *linear* classifier.

Nothing on this page involves TensorFlow yet; it is plain NumPy and Matplotlib. The model variables, forward pass, loss and training step follow on pp.95-96.

paragraphs.excerpt: negative_samples and positive_samples are both arrays with shape (1000, 2).
paragraphs.what_it_says: The two arrays created in listing 3.13 each have shape `(1000, 2)`, and the next step is to stack them into a single array of shape `(2000, 2)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each array holds 1,000 samples (rows), and each sample has 2 features (columns): its x and y coordinate. A model trains on one input array, not one array per class, so the two classes have to be merged into a single tensor whose first axis is the sample axis. Stacking along the rows keeps the feature axis untouched (still 2) and adds up the sample counts (1000 + 1000 = 2000).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the batch/sample axis convention introduced in chapter 2: axis 0 indexes samples, the remaining axes describe one sample. Getting it right here is what lets `matmul(inputs, W)` on p.95 process all 2,000 points in one operation.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Concatenation along axis 0 requires all other axes to match; two `(1000, 2)` arrays can be stacked, but a `(1000, 2)` and a `(1000, 3)` array could not.

terminology.meaning: The tuple of axis lengths of an array; `(1000, 2)` means 1,000 rows and 2 columns (p.47).
Place arrays one on top of the other so that their rows are concatenated.

connections: p.93: listing 3.13 creates negative_samples and positive_samples with np.random.multivariate_normal, 1,000 points each.
p.47: shape and dtype are two of the three key attributes of a tensor.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let's generate the corresponding target labels, an array of 0s and 1s
paragraphs.what_it_says: The targets are an array of 0s and 1s with shape `(2000, 1)`, where `targets[i, 0]` is 0 if `inputs[i]` belongs to class 0, and 1 if it belongs to class 1.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Supervised learning needs one label per input, in the same order. Because the inputs were stacked negatives-first, the labels must also be zeros-first: rows 0-999 get 0 and rows 1000-1999 get 1. The shape is `(2000, 1)` rather than `(2000,)` so that each label is itself a vector of length 1, matching the model's output shape (one prediction value per sample in a column).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: If the label order did not match the input order, the model would be trained on garbage pairs. And if the target shape did not match the prediction shape, the subtraction `targets - predictions` in the loss (p.95) would broadcast `(2000,)` against `(2000, 1)` into a `(2000, 2000)` matrix, a silent and classic bug.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Using 0 and 1 as numeric targets lets the authors treat classification as regression: the model outputs a real number, is trained with mean squared error, and later a threshold of 0.5 decides the class (p.96).

terminology.meaning: The value the model should output for a given input; here, the class index 0 or 1 stored as a float.
The two categories; class 0 is the 'negative' samples, class 1 the 'positive' samples.

connections: p.95: the mean squared error loss compares targets with predictions element-wise.
p.96: predictions are classified as 1 if above 0.5 and 0 otherwise.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let's plot our data with Matplotlib, a well-known Python data visualization library
paragraphs.what_it_says: The data are plotted with Matplotlib, which is preinstalled in Colab, producing figure 3.1.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Before training anything, the authors look at the data. A scatter plot of 2D points colored by class shows directly whether the classes overlap, how they are shaped, and whether a straight line could separate them.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Visual inspection is cheap and catches errors early (wrong labels, swapped columns, unexpected outliers). It also sets up the payoff on p.97, where the learned decision line is drawn over this same plot.

terminology.meaning: The standard Python plotting library; `matplotlib.pyplot` (conventionally imported as `plt`) provides a MATLAB-style plotting interface.

concepts.name: Synthetic, linearly separable data
concepts.definition: Artificially generated data whose structure you control; here, two Gaussian point clouds in 2D that a straight line can mostly separate.
concepts.intuition: When learning a new tool you want a problem where you already know the answer, so that if training fails you know it is the code, not the data.
concepts.technical: Each class is drawn from a 2D normal distribution with the same covariance `[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]` and different means, `[0, 3]` and `[3, 0]` (p.93). With equal covariances, the optimal decision boundary between two Gaussians is a straight line, which is exactly what a linear classifier can represent.
concepts.significance: It makes the end-to-end example small enough to understand line by line while still exercising every piece of a real training loop.
concepts.example: Figure 3.1: purple blob near (0, 3), yellow blob near (3, 0).
concepts.misconception: Linearly separable does not mean perfectly separable here: the blobs overlap slightly at the boundary, so even the best line misclassifies a few points.

concepts.name: Stacking arrays along the sample axis
concepts.definition: Concatenating several arrays along axis 0 so that their samples form one larger dataset; `np.vstack` does this for 2D arrays.
concepts.intuition: Like putting two spreadsheets with the same columns one under the other.
concepts.technical: `np.vstack((a, b))` with `a.shape == (n1, d)` and `b.shape == (n2, d)` returns shape `(n1 + n2, d)`. It is equivalent to `np.concatenate((a, b), axis=0)` for 2D inputs. The order of the tuple determines the order of rows in the result.
concepts.significance: Inputs and targets must be stacked in the same order so that row i of one corresponds to row i of the other.
concepts.example: `np.vstack((negative_samples, positive_samples))` turns two `(1000, 2)` arrays into a `(2000, 2)` array.
concepts.misconception: `np.vstack` is not the same as `np.stack`: `np.stack` would create a new axis and return `(2, 1000, 2)`.

concepts.name: Tensor shape and dtype
concepts.definition: An n-dimensional array characterized by its rank, shape and data type (p.47).
concepts.intuition: The shape tells you how the numbers are organized; the dtype tells you what kind of numbers they are.
concepts.technical: Here `inputs` is a rank-2 float32 tensor of shape `(2000, 2)` and `targets` is a rank-2 float32 tensor of shape `(2000, 1)`. The cast to float32 matters because NumPy defaults to float64, and TensorFlow does not silently mix dtypes in operations such as `tf.matmul`.
concepts.significance: Shape and dtype mismatches are the most common source of errors when feeding NumPy data into a deep learning framework.
concepts.misconception: float32 is not chosen for accuracy; it is chosen because it is the standard precision for deep learning on GPUs and halves memory compared with float64.

code.title: Stacking the two classes into an array with shape (2000, 2)
code.what_it_does: Concatenates the 1,000 class-0 points and the 1,000 class-1 points into one `(2000, 2)` array and converts it to 32-bit floats.

line_explanations.explanation: `np.vstack` takes a tuple of arrays and stacks them row-wise; negatives come first (rows 0-999), positives after (rows 1000-1999). `.astype(np.float32)` returns a float32 copy, since `multivariate_normal` produces float64.

code.algorithm: Row-wise concatenation followed by a dtype cast.
code.theory_link: Axis 0 is the samples axis; each row is a 2-feature sample (x, y). The model on p.95 multiplies this whole matrix by `W` of shape (2, 1) in one call.

parameters.name: (negative_samples, positive_samples)
parameters.role: The arrays to stack; their order fixes the order of rows and must match the order used for targets.

parameters.name: np.float32
parameters.role: Target dtype, matching the float32 variables used in TensorFlow.

pitfalls: Forgetting the cast leaves float64 data, and `tf.matmul` with a float32 variable then raises a dtype error.
Note the double parentheses: `np.vstack` takes a single tuple argument, not two separate arrays.
code.illustrative_code:
# Beyond the book: equivalent forms and a shape check
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((1000, 2)); b = np.ones((1000, 2))
print(np.vstack((a, b)).shape)              # (2000, 2)
print(np.concatenate((a, b), axis=0).shape)  # (2000, 2)
print(np.stack((a, b)).shape)                # (2, 1000, 2)  -- not what we want

code.title: Generating the corresponding targets (0 and 1)
code.what_it_does: Builds a `(2000, 1)` float32 column of labels: 1,000 zeros followed by 1,000 ones, aligned with the rows of `inputs`.

line_explanations.explanation: Call `np.vstack` on a tuple (the opening parenthesis on line 2 starts the tuple).
`np.zeros((1000, 1), dtype="float32")`: one label 0 per class-0 sample, as a column vector.
`np.ones((1000, 1), dtype="float32")`: one label 1 per class-1 sample.
Close the tuple and the call; the result has shape `(2000, 1)`.

code.algorithm: Create a constant block per class and stack them in the same order as the inputs.
code.theory_link: Encoding the two classes as 0 and 1 lets the classifier be trained with mean squared error and thresholded at 0.5 later (pp.95-96).

parameters.name: num_samples_per_class
parameters.role: Number of rows per block; must equal the number of samples generated per class.

parameters.name: dtype="float32"
parameters.role: Makes the labels float32 so they can be subtracted from float32 predictions in the loss.

pitfalls: Swapping the order of zeros and ones would mislabel every point.
Using shape `(num_samples_per_class,)` instead of `(num_samples_per_class, 1)` would produce `(2000,)` targets, which broadcast incorrectly against `(2000, 1)` predictions.
code.illustrative_code:
# Beyond the book: two equivalent one-liners
import numpy as np
n = 1000
t1 = np.concatenate([np.zeros((n, 1)), np.ones((n, 1))]).astype("float32")
t2 = np.repeat([0.0, 1.0], n).reshape(-1, 1).astype("float32")
assert (t1 == t2).all() and t1.shape == (2000, 1)

`inputs[:, 0]` is the first column (all x coordinates, shape (2000,)), `inputs[:, 1]` the second column (all y coordinates). `c=targets[:, 0]` passes the 2,000 labels as a 1D array of numbers that Matplotlib maps to colors through its default colormap (viridis: 0 is dark purple, 1 is yellow).

code.theory_link: Slicing `[:, j]` selects feature j for all samples, the same tensor-slicing idea seen in chapter 2.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
for label, color in [(0, "purple"), (1, "gold")]:
    mask = targets[:, 0] == label
    plt.scatter(inputs[mask, 0], inputs[mask, 1], c=color, s=8, label=f"class {label}")
plt.gca().set_aspect("equal")

plt.show()

deeper.title: Why a straight line should work on this data
deeper.body: Beyond the book: both classes were sampled (p.93) from Gaussians with the **same** covariance matrix $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.5\\ 0.5 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and means $\mu_0 = (0, 3)$ and $\mu_1 = (3, 0)$. For two Gaussians with equal covariance and equal priors, the Bayes-optimal boundary is linear: it is the set of points where $(\mu_1-\mu_0)^\top \Sigma^{-1} x$ equals a constant. Here $\mu_1 - \mu_0 = (3, -3)$ and $\Sigma^{-1}(3,-3)^\top = (6, -6)$, so the boundary is of the form $x - y = c$, and by symmetry it passes through the midpoint $(1.5, 1.5)$: the line $y = x$. That matches what you see in figure 3.1: a diagonal gap running from lower left to upper right. The model trained on pp.95-96 learns a line close to this one.

deeper.title: The positive correlation inside each blob
deeper.body: Beyond the book: the off-diagonal 0.5 in the covariance gives each cloud a correlation of 0.5 between x and y, which is why the blobs in figure 3.1 are elongated along the direction (1, 1), from lower left to upper right. Since that is also the direction of the separating line $y = x$, the clouds are stretched *parallel* to the boundary, so few points cross it. If the covariance were `[[1, -0.5], [-0.5, 1]]`, the clouds would be stretched toward each other and the overlap would be larger.

deeper.title: Shapes through the whole example
deeper.body:
1. `negative_samples`, `positive_samples`: `(1000, 2)` each (p.93).
2. `inputs = np.vstack(...)`: `(2000, 2)` (this page).
3. `targets`: `(2000, 1)` (this page).
4. `W`: `(2, 1)`, `b`: `(1,)` (p.95).
5. `predictions = matmul(inputs, W) + b`: `(2000, 2)·(2, 1) = (2000, 1)`, plus `b` broadcast (p.95).
6. `targets - predictions`: `(2000, 1)`; its mean squared value is the loss (a scalar).

The target shape on this page was chosen precisely so that step 6 is an element-wise subtraction of two same-shaped tensors.

visualizations.title: Shape flow from the two classes to the training arrays
visualizations.why: Listings 3.14 and 3.15 stack two (1000, 2) arrays into (2000, 2) inputs and two (1000, 1) blocks into (2000, 1) targets; this shows how those shapes feed the model on the next page.

misconceptions.claim: `np.vstack((a, b))` with two (1000, 2) arrays gives a (2, 1000, 2) array.
misconceptions.correction: That is what `np.stack` does. `np.vstack` concatenates rows of 2D arrays, giving (2000, 2).

misconceptions.claim: The targets could just as well be a flat array of shape (2000,).
misconceptions.correction: The book uses (2000, 1) to match the (2000, 1) predictions. With (2000,), `targets - predictions` would broadcast to (2000, 2000) and the loss would be wrong without any error.

misconceptions.claim: The two classes in figure 3.1 are perfectly separable.
misconceptions.correction: They overlap a little near the middle; a linear classifier separates them well but not perfectly.
All three listings are pure NumPy and Matplotlib; TensorFlow variables are introduced on p.95.

takeaways: Inputs from all classes are stacked into one array whose axis 0 is the sample axis: two (1000, 2) arrays become one (2000, 2) array.
Targets must be built in exactly the same row order as the inputs; here 1,000 zeros followed by 1,000 ones, shape (2000, 1).
Cast NumPy data to float32 before handing it to TensorFlow; NumPy's random generators produce float64.
The (2000, 1) target shape is chosen to match the model's (2000, 1) predictions, avoiding accidental broadcasting in the loss.
Plotting the data first (figure 3.1) shows two tilted Gaussian blobs that a straight line can mostly separate, which is why a linear classifier is appropriate.

questions.question: What is the shape of `np.vstack((negative_samples, positive_samples))` when both arrays have shape (1000, 2)?
questions.explanation: `vstack` concatenates along the rows (axis 0), so the row counts add up and the column count stays 2. (1000, 4) would be `hstack` (columns concatenated), (2, 1000, 2) would be `np.stack` (new leading axis), and (1000, 2, 2) would be stacking along a new last axis.

questions.question: Why does listing 3.14 call `.astype(np.float32)`?
questions.answer: Because `np.random.multivariate_normal` returns float64 data, while the TensorFlow model variables and operations in this example are float32; the cast makes the dtypes compatible.
questions.explanation: TensorFlow does not implicitly mix float64 and float32 in ops like `tf.matmul`; float32 is also the standard deep-learning precision (TensorFlow tensors default to float32, p.88).

questions.question: What would go wrong if listing 3.15 stacked the ones before the zeros, while listing 3.14 kept negatives first?
questions.answer: Every label would be flipped: class-0 points would be labeled 1 and vice versa.
questions.explanation: The correspondence between inputs and targets is purely positional: `targets[i, 0]` describes `inputs[i]`. Flipping the order of one but not the other inverts all labels. The model would still learn a line, but it would predict the opposite class names, which is a silent bug.

questions.question: The targets have shape (2000, 1) rather than (2000,). What could happen in the loss computation `targets - predictions` if they were (2000,) while predictions are (2000, 1)?
questions.answer: Broadcasting would produce a (2000, 2000) matrix of differences, so the mean squared error would be computed over all pairs of samples instead of matching pairs, without raising an error.
questions.explanation: Broadcasting aligns trailing axes: (2000,) is treated as (1, 2000) and (2000, 1) is expanded across columns, giving (2000, 2000). Matching shapes, as the book chooses, avoid this.

questions.question: In listing 3.16, what does `inputs[:, 1]` select?
options: The y coordinates of all samples
questions.answer: The y coordinates of all samples
questions.explanation: `:` on axis 0 keeps every row, `1` on axis 1 picks the second column, which holds the y coordinate of each point. The second sample would be `inputs[1]`; labels live in `targets`; the first 1,000 samples would be `inputs[:1000]`.

questions.question: Looking at figure 3.1, roughly where are the two classes centered, and what in listing 3.13 determines that?
questions.answer: One class (dark) is centered near (0, 3) and the other (yellow) near (3, 0); these are the `mean` arguments passed to `np.random.multivariate_normal` on p.93.
questions.explanation: The scatter plot is a direct picture of the sampling distributions; the shared covariance `[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]` explains the tilted, elongated shape of both clouds.

questions.question: Without looking, write the three listings on this page from memory, then check the shapes of `inputs` and `targets` by printing `.shape` and `.dtype`.
questions.explanation: Being able to prepare and sanity-check aligned input/target arrays is the prerequisite for every training loop in the book, starting with the one on pp.95-96.
